# **Platinum group metals** 

_Notes on Johnson Matthey’s latest review of the platinum group metal markets._ 

**David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** 

**15 November 2011** 

#### **New York:** 

- Johnson Matthey Plc’s latest report (Platinum 2011 Interim Review) covering the fundamentals of the platinum group metals markets throughout 2011 was released earlier today (on the 15th of November). As we expected, they reported that the platinum market should be in a surplus of 195,000 ounces for 2011 as a whole. The figures for the palladium market indicate that palladium too is expected to be in a surplus, of 725,000 ounces. 

- According to Johnson Matthey, the platinum market is expected to be in surplus by 195,000 ounces in 2011 and to be in a smaller surplus in 2012. Industrial demand has been at record levels and underlying fundamentals look relatively positive. 

• The palladium market is expected to move from a deficit of 530,000 ounces in 2010 to a surplus of 725,000 ounces in 2011. In large part, this change has been driven by the switch by ETF investors from net buying last year to net selling this year. Without the estimated 750,000 ounces of Russian state stock sales this market would nonetheless be in deficit this year. Industrial and automotive demand have  increased. Primary (mine) and secondary (recycling) production have both increased to limit the scale of this year’s surplus. Palladium is likely to be in deficit next year. 

- Johnson Matthey’s price forecast for the next six months is relatively neutral compared to today’s prices. Platinum is expected to trade between $1,450 and $1,800 and palladium to trade between $500 and $800. This is much less bullish than the forecast of six months ago, reflecting weak economic conditions. 

- According to Johnson Matthey’s figures, the rhodium market is likely to be in surplus again in 2011. The forecast is for a surplus of 123,000 ounces, somewhat higher than was seen last year. Although no market balance was reported for iridium and ruthenium, demand figures suggest a slowdown in ruthenium demand compared to 2010 and a slight improvement in iridium demand.

## **<mark>Platinum</mark>** 

Johnson Matthey’s (JM) most recent estimates for the platinum market suggest that gross demand for platinum is expected to grow by 2.2 per cent to 8.08 million ounces, close to pre-crisis levels, in 2011. Open loop recycling should increase by

2.7 per cent to 1.88 million ounces and metal sales from primary mining are set to expand by 5.7 per cent to 6.40 million ounces. Overall, the market is set to move from close to balance last year into a surplus of 195,000 ounces for the year. 

Gross platinum demand from the automotive sector is set to increase this year, rising by 2.8 per cent to 3.16 million ounces. Although the European car market has been weak this year, with widespread economic problems depressing consumers’ willingness to buy new vehicles, the market share of the diesel vehicle increased. Substitution of some of the platinum in a typical diesel catalyst by palladium is continuing and Johnson Matthey expects some 30 per cent of the diesel catalyst market by weight to be palladium this year (with slow progress towards perhaps a fifty per cent share for palladium in a decade’s time). Light duty vehicle platinum demand is expected to be little changed from last year. 

Outside Europe, platinum demand depends on the growth of the diesel car segment, given that gasoline (or three way) catalysts are now almost exclusively palladium/rhodium based. Growth in North American and Indian diesel passenger car sales is therefore positive for platinum demand. Growth in heavy duty diesel vehicle production (up by almost half in North America this year) is now a major component of automotive demand. 

Gross jewellery sector demand for platinum is expected to rise by roughly 1.9 per cent to 2.47 million ounces this year. The North American market has been fairly healthy but European demand has weakened a little. Gross Japanese demand will fall marginally but has been much stronger than might have been expected given the triple disaster that occurred in Q2 2011. More metal will be recycled in Japan, though, than in the previous year. 

However, the most important market remains China. Here, the narrowing (and recent reversal) of platinum’s traditional price differential with gold has been too recent to allow a simple forecast of consumer or manufacturer behaviour. As Zhou Enlai said of the French Revolution’s impact, “It is too early to say”. We note, however, from Mitsui’s own research and Johnson Matthey’s comments, that some of the production capacity that would normally be available for platinum jewellery manufacturing has been diverted to gold production. In our view, this places a limit on the potential output of the platinum jewellery manufacturers in the short term. Overall, Johnson Matthey’s figures indicate that this individual market could grow from a gross 1.65 million ounces to 1.69 million ounces this year. We believe that the market could grow a little faster than this. Recycling rates have fallen so net demand for new metal has risen by roughly ten per cent. 

Industrial demand for platinum should reach a record level following the previous year’s strong growth. It should increase by 11.7 per cent to 1.96 million ounces. Despite gloomladen headlines, the world’s economy has g

rown this year and there has been a reasonable amount of investment in new capacity for the electronics and chemical industry. In China, a crackdown on credit availability has restricted new building and infrastructure construction, limiting metal requirements from the fibre glass industry. However, investment in additional Asian flat panel glass construction capacity added additional demand for platinum this year. 

Identifiable physical investment demand is set to decrease significantly, falling from 655,000 ounces to 495,000 ounces, according to Johnson Matthey. Although the nature of this market makes forecasting harder than in many other sectors, ETF investor selling has been an important force this year. Compared to last year, this has been, overall, much less significant although there have been spells of strong buying and selling. The high prices of mid-2011 also drew a confusion of buying and selling in the Japanese physical investment market. As a result, the investment market showed its true spots as an influence on the price rather than a true part of the supply/demand fundamental equation.

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Platinum Group Metals** 

**15 November 2011** 

The weight of platinum recovered from open loop recycling of autocatalysts, electronics and jewellery looks likely to increase by 2.7 per cent to 1.88 million ounces, higher than last year’s figure, but with growth rates having slowed. Most of the growth in recycling of platinum has come from the automotive sector, with the return to more normal patterns of car buying within Europe following the end of the range of national scrappage schemes that followed the start of the global economic crisis. Jewellery recycling decreased by 45,000 ounces as less metal was recovered in China from this source, while Japanese consumers sold more second hand jewellery in the form of scrap. 

The weight of platinum set to be sold by the mining sector is likely to rise by 5.7 per cent to 6.40 million ounces. Primary supplies of platinum from Russia should remain close to 825,000 ounces. North American platinum production should climb, following the end of prolonged industrial action at some of the nickel mines in Sudbury and a full year of operations at North American Palladium’s Lac des Iles mine. 

Southern African output is also expected to grow. Despite the political uncertainty and longer term concerns brought about by the indigenisation process, recent expansions at the three operating mines in Zimbabwe should see output climb by a fifth to 335,000 ounces. Platinum supplies from South Africa should climb from 4.64 million ounces last year to 4.78 million ounces in 2011 despite some strikes and safety stoppages. 

However, the outlook for platinum production in the short to medium term is perhaps more interesting. The recent weakness in the platinum price and continued cost inflation means that profitability can only be readily addressed by a weaker Rand, high

er output to control unit costs, higher by-product prices or the closure or mothballing of more expensive operations. To date, there has been little rationalisation of supply and the economics of individual companies may mean that this is slow to occur. Johnson Matthey’s view is that South African mine supply has the potential to expand further next year. 

In fact, looking into 2012, platinum supplies should grow if South African and Zimbabwean production meet their targets. JM expects to see further growth on the demand side with the Chinese jewellery market expected to remain healthy although it is still too early to forecast the impact on demand of the recent price premium for gold over platinum. The economic outlook is rather uncertain and the outlook for automotive and industrial demand for platinum is correspondingly unclear. However, JM gave some indications of what they believe the potential for the heavy duty and off-road catalyst market could be in terms of demand. They stated that these will use as much as 480,000 ounces and 130,000 ounces respectively this year, making these significant new sources of demand with further legislation-driven growth anticiapted 

Platinum should weather weak economic growth due to its “strong fundamentals” with heavy duty and off-road demand selected as important drivers. Finally, “platinum will”, apparently, “be in surplus again in 2012 but not by a significant amount. Platinum is forecast to trade between $1,450 and $1,800 in the next six month period.

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Platinum Group Metals** 

**15 November 2011** 

## **<mark>Palladium</mark>** 

Johnson Matthey’s latest report estimates that gross demand for palladium will shrink by 8.7 per cent to 8.89 million ounces this year, with net selling of ETF metal primarily responsible for the year-on-year change. Over the last two years, ETF flows have been substantial and have outweighed the more fundamental parts of the supply and demand equation. Taking ETF flows out from both 2010 and 2011 reveals that “there is strong underlying industrial demand”, a more reasonable view of the health of the market. 

On the supply side, strong growth in recycling of autocatalysts is set to help boost reclamation of palladium by 18.6 per cent to 2.20 million ounces this year. At the same time, mine supplies of palladium are expected to grow by 4.7 per cent to 6.67 million ounces. Johnson Matthey’s expectations are that sales of Russian state stock material could total some 750,000 ounces this year, three quarters of last year’s figure. 

Overall, therefore, JM believes that the palladium market is to move back from last year’s deficit of 530,000 ounces into a surplus of 725,000 ounces this year. Excluding ETF material flows and Russian state stock figures from the equation might give a truer picture of the state of this market and would indicate that 2010 and 2011 were quite similar in terms of other supply and demand. 

Despit

e the overt bearishness of ETF investors, the forecast price for the next six months has palladium trading between $500 and $800, a relatively neutral outlook. Looking further into the future, JM sees the palladium market tightening with “the palladium market likely to be in deficit next year”. 

In the automotive market, palladium use has increased this year and is expected to rise from 5.58 million ounces in 2010 to 5.92 million ounces, a record level. Despite the gloom pervading much of the global economy, the Chinese car market has grown (albeit significantly more slowly than was the case last year) and loadings have increased too with palladium use rising by almost ten per cent. European output is healthier than might have been expected (in part to supply China’s luxury vehicle requirements) and the North American market has continued its slow recovery. With palladium still gradually eroding platinum’s dominance in the diesel sector (it is now 30 per cent of the metal on a typical catalyst), palladium demand has therefore strengthened. 

Economic growth, no matter how wobbly, has also boosted palladium use in the electronics sector where demand has increased by 75,000 ounces to 1.49 million ounces. Chemical industry demand for palladium has also expanded compared to one year ago as requirements for compounds such as purified terephthalic acid have grown. In the dental sector, the high price of gold has had some positive effects on the North American market (where palladium is typically used in low gold content alloys) but a negative impact in the Japanese market (where it is employed in higher gold content alloys). The overall impact has been neutral in terms of demand for palladium from this sector. 

Jewellery demand looks set to disappoint. European jewellery demand is steady but North American requirements for palladium are set to fall as the lower end of the industry takes part in a “race to the bottom” by replacing precious metals with cheaper materials. In other markets such as Japan, palladium has not yet reached a level of widespread availability or mass consumer awareness. The most important market, though, for palladium jewellery remains China. As Mitsui’s own research shows, manufacturing demand has been dwindling for some time and this year is expected to see a further 30,000 ounces decline to 330,000 ounces (from a global jewellery demand of 545,000 ounces). 

Identifiable physical investment demand has changed from being a mover for higher prices and a tighter market in 2010 to a source of metal to the market and a drag on prices in 2011. North American investors in particular have been net sellers of metal. On its own, the 1.31 million ounce swing in metal flows from last year to this year is responsible for almost all of the net change in the supply and demand picture. Johnson Matthey attributes the difference between investor behaviour in platinum and palladium to two facts: palladium’s

stunning price performance last year made profit-taking possible for many investors; and palladium’s perception “as a purer industrial play” which is more subject to fears of an economic slowdown. 

On the supply side, primary production has been relatively little different compared to initial expectations. Sales of mined metal and material from state stocks are expected to rise from 7.36 million ounces in 2010 to 7.42 million ounces this year. South African supplies of palladium will fall marginally to 2.61 million ounces. Russian output should be close to stable at 2.7 million ounces. There will be growth in supplies of palladium from Zimbabwe. North American supplies should climb by sixty per cent to 945,000 ounces. Improved grades at Stillwater and North American Palladium and the return to normal operation of Vale’s Sudbury nickel mines following an extended strike are the major contributors to the increase in palladium production in this latter region. 

Johnson Matthey separates out its forecast of Russian state stock sales. It believes these will fall from last year’s estimate of one million ounces to 750,000 ounces this year. In answer to a question over future shipments, they referred to recent reports that Gokhran, the state repository, is planning to export only 4 to 4.5 tonnes of palladium in each of the next two years. Without any Russian state exports this year, the palladium market would have been almost balanced. 

Recycling recoveries have been boosted from 1.85 million ounces last year and should reach 2.20 million ounces this year. Electronic scrap recoveries will climb by almost a tenth, driven by environmental legislation. Jewellery recovery will double as more unsold stock is returned from manufacturers and retailers within China. Autocatalyst recoveries are also strong and should climb by 15 per cent to 1.51 million ounces. 

The outlook is for “tighter supplies in 2012 due to substantially lower Russian state stock sales”. Automotive demand growth should apparently be as strong in 2012 as it has been in 2011 assuming that the economic situation does not deteriorate rapidly. Industrial demand should remain healthy too. Finally, “even with some Russian stock sales and increased autocatalyst recycling, the palladium market is likely to be in a deficit next year”. 

## **<mark>Other pgm</mark>** 

Rhodium was covered briefly in the presentation. Mine supply is set to increase from 734,000 ounces to 768,000 ounces this year due to higher refined output from the South African producers. Supplies from other countries will rise marginally. Recycling of rhodium is set to grow from 241,000 ounces to 260,000 ounces as rhodium loadings on scrapped cars continue to increase. Rhodium demand will grow too, rising by 18,000 ounces to 905,000 ounces. Gross autocatalyst demand is expected to shrink by 3 per cent to 705,000 ounces due to thrifting of metal, the triple disast

er in Japan and a decrease in the market share of the gasoline vehicle within Europe. Fortunately, chemical demand will grow and glass makers have added LCD glass manufacturing capacity and have increased the rhodium content of many of the alloys they use. 

Overall, the rhodium market will see its surplus increase from 88,000 ounces last year to 123,000 ounces this year. Looking forward, the rhodium market is expected “to tighten but remain in surplus” suggesting that upwards price pressures may not be too apparent in the next twelve months on fundamental grounds at least. 

No market balance is reported for ruthenium or iridium. However, ruthenium demand has shrunk from 945,000 ounces a year ago to this year’s 811,000 ounces due to lower stockbuilding by the hard disk industry. Iridium demand will be almost flat at 342,000 ounces
